column4: Last lesson you built the launchpad. You opened a brokerage account, picked a broker, and saw how options approval levels keep beginners out of trades they aren't ready for. So the account is open and the money is sitting there. One question is left, the one this whole course has been walking toward. How do you actually place the trade? Welcome to the finale. Today you learn the three order types every investor uses, how to read the gap between buyers and sellers, and the six point checklist that turns a guess into a plan. By the end, you'll know exactly what to tap, and in what order, before a single real dollar moves.

Every order starts with one decision: how should this fill? Watch the price line on the diagram. Say the stock trades at fifty dollars. A market order says, fill me now. It executes right away at the best current price, maybe a touch above or below fifty. Speed is guaranteed, price is not. Now place a limit order at forty nine. That says, fill me at forty nine or better, not a penny worse. Price is guaranteed, the fill is not. If the stock never dips to forty nine, the order simply waits. Last, set a stop at forty seven. Nothing happens until price touches forty seven. The moment it does, the stop wakes up and becomes a market order, usually to get you out before a slide gets worse. So market trades price for speed, limit trades speed for price, and a stop is your automatic exit.

Before any order fills, two prices are staring at each other. The bid is the highest price a buyer is offering right now. The ask is the lowest price a seller will accept. Look at the two hands on screen reaching toward each other. That small gap between them is the spread. Say the bid is forty nine dollars and ninety five cents, and the ask is fifty dollars and five cents. The spread is ten cents. A narrow spread like that means a liquid market, plenty of buyers and sellers packed close together, so your order fills near the price you see. A wide spread means fewer players and worse fills. Glance at the spread before you trade. It tells you how crowded the room is.

Open any stock's quote page and you meet the same wall of tiles. Good news: you already know most of them. Price is what it trades for right now, and open is where it started the day. Bid and ask you just learned. Volume counts the shares changing hands, and more volume means easier fills. The P E ratio compares price to earnings, and E P S is the profit behind each share, both from the fundamentals week. Market cap is the whole company's price tag. The fifty two week range shows the year's high and low, so you can see where today sits. And beta gauges how sharply the stock swings compared to the whole market. Scan the chips on screen. If you can say one plain sentence about each tile, you're reading the dashboard, not just staring at it.

Here is the pre flight ritual. A first trade earns takeoff only when six boxes are checked. Your thesis, the one sentence reason you want this company. Your entry, the price you're willing to pay. Your stop, the exit that caps the loss. Your size, risking only one to two percent of the account. Your exit plan for taking profits. And your order type, usually a limit, so you control the price. Quick check before you tap: which of the six caps your worst case loss? That's the stop. Now tap all six boxes on screen yourself, and when the last one clicks, you'll see the words every new investor should live by.

Time to sort like a pro. On screen are eight first trade behaviors. Tap a card, then tap the column where it belongs. One column holds smart first trade habits, the discipline this course has been building. The other holds rookie mistakes, the shortcuts that cost real money. As you sort, notice the pattern. Every smart habit decides something before the trade. Every mistake skips that decision.
Last quiz of the course. Five questions. Lock in what you've learned.

That's the course. Look how far you've come. You know why compounding rewards patience, what a share really is, how to read statements and charts, how funds spread risk, how options work, how to size a trade and manage your own mind, and now, how to place the order itself. One instruction remains, the most important one on this page. Paper trade the plan before going live. Run the full checklist on a practice account, thesis, entry, stop, size, exit, order type, until the ritual feels boring. Boring is the goal. When real money finally moves, it follows a plan you've already rehearsed. Keep practicing, keep journaling, and keep your risk small. You're cleared for takeoff.
